title: EDUCATION | 5.24.26 Am I Doing It Wrong? (On Mortimer Adler's How to Read a Book)
author: Connor Wondrasch
summary: A PhD student halfway through his program discovers Mortimer Adler's How to Read a Book and confronts an uncomfortable realization: he has been reading academically for years without reading analytically or synoptically. Prompted by a YouTube video titled 'I did a PhD without knowing how to read,' Wondrasch buys Adler's 1940 classic (updated 1972) and reads it in three days. He reflects on how Ryan Holiday, Robert Greene, Sonke Ahrens, and Mike Schmitz had taught him various note-taking and linking methods, but Adler teaches the foundational skill they all presuppose: active, demanding reading aimed at genuine understanding rather than information extraction. Adler's four levels -- elementary (decoding), inspectional (systematic skimming), analytical (thorough understanding of one book), and synoptical (reading across multiple sources on a topic) -- form a hierarchy where each level subsumes the previous. Wondrasch argues that education's hyperfocus on elementary (basic literacy) has created an artificial ceiling, leaving higher-order reading underdeveloped in most students and, evidently, many graduate scholars.
points: * Adler's four levels of reading -- elementary, inspectional, analytical, and synoptical -- form a cumulative hierarchy: most readers plateau at elementary or inspectional, even those completing advanced degrees. * The distinction between reading for information and reading for understanding is foundational: information-seeking is passive; understanding requires active, demanding engagement with the author's argument -- asking and answering the book's central questions. * Education's hyperfocus on elementary reading (basic decoding and literacy) since the 1970s has, per Adler, created an artificial glass ceiling that leaves inspectional, analytical, and synoptical reading underdeveloped. * Wondrasch synthesizes Adler with Ryan Holiday (mark your books), Robert Greene (notecards), Sonke Ahrens (smart, atomic notes), and Mike Schmitz (linked thinking) -- Adler provides the reading substrate that makes all the other systems work. * Transfer is the key test of understanding: being able to use knowledge in new contexts proves genuine comprehension -- and demanding, active reading is what builds the depth necessary for transfer.
quotes: I am not the same. Because I read a book. Not just any book, mind you. A book that I should have read much sooner in my PhD journey, even in my life as a student in general.
Transfer, of course, is the point of all our reading and thinking -- we want to be able to understand and transfer is the best evidence to be declared guilty of understanding.
How we read is just as important as what we read. -- Mortimer Adler
Reading is hard and should be quite active. The way that we typically read for pleasure, relaxation, or information is not the same way that we should be reading for proper understanding.
Our hyper focus on making sure every student or child makes it to [elementary reading] has created an artificial glass ceiling for the other levels of reading. -- Mortimer Adler
